The writer uses language to make the discovery of
the violin exciting by highlighting the emotions that
John is feeling as the passage progresses. He uses
phrases indicating strong emotions such as “a
feverish anxiety” (Line 18) and “reached an
overmastering pitch” (Line 23­24).
The writer gives details of John’s emotional up and
down (written in longer paragraphs) to make the
discovery of the violin exciting. We see John
excited with anticipation as he realizes that there is
something behind the picture frame. “His curiosity
was excited …” (line 14). This excitement mounts
as he works to open the mysterious hidden
cupboard. “… his heart beat so fast that he could
scarcely catch his breath …” (line 32). Once the
cupboard is open we see this excitement dissipate
almost immediately when John concludes that the
cupboard has nothing more than dust and cobwebs
in it. “His sense of disappointment was keen as he
thrust his hand into it …” (Line 35­36). This
disappointment is fleeting when he puts his hand
into the cupboard and feels something solid. “John
was excited at his discovery, and felt his thoughts
confused.” (Line 44). His breathless excitement
returns as he works to find a light and to remove the
object in order to discover what it is. “The extreme
beauty of its varnish impressed him vividly …”
(Line 68) / “he felt a conviction gradually gaining
…” (Line 69).
In addition to the words that describe John`s
excitement the writer also provides many words that
leave the reader wondering about what John found.
We are left wondering as we walk step by step
through the discovery alongside John. For example,
when John removes the violin from the cupboard
the writer describes it as being covered with “the
curious drapery of black and clinging cobwebs”
(Line 40). John then moves the instrument with
great care “as he feared lest age should have
rendered the wood brittle or rotten” (Line 47­48).
Before John opens the case, he clears the thick
cobwebs “with some vigorous puffs of breath and a
little dusting with a handkerchief “ (Line 48­49).
Finally, he takes the violin out after “A few minutes
more gentle handling” (Line 51).

 At last the horses began to go more slowly, as if they were climbing up-hill, and presently there 
seemed to be no more hedges and no more trees.  She could see nothing, in fact, but a dense darkness on 
either side.  She leaned forward and pressed her face against the window just as the carriage gave a big 
jolt. 
 “Eh! We’re on the moor now sure enough,” said Mrs. Medlock. 
 The carriage lamps shed a yellow light on a rough-looking road which seemed to be cut through 
bushes and low-growing things which ended in the great expanse of dark apparently spread out before  
and around them.  A wind was rising and making a singular, wild, low, rushing sound. 
 “It’ s—it’ s not the sea, is it?” said Mary, looking round at her companion. 
 “No, not it,” answered Mrs. Medlock.  “Nor it isn’t fields nor mountains, it’ s just miles and miles and 
miles of wild land that nothing grows on but heather and gorse and broom, and nothing lives on but wild 
ponies and sheep.” 
 “I feel as if it might be the sea, if there were water on it,” said Mary.  “It sounds like the sea just now.” 
 “That’ s the wind blowing through the bushes,” Mrs. Medlock said.  “It’ s a wild, dreary enough place 
to my mind, though there’ s plenty that likes it—particularly when the heather’ s in bloom.” 
 On and on they drove through the darkness, and though the rain stopped, the wind rushed by and 
whistled and made strange sounds.  The road went up and down, and several times the carriage passed 
over a little bridge beneath which water rushed very fast with a great deal of noise.  Mary felt as if the 
drive would never come to an end and that the wide, bleak moor was a wide expanse of black ocean 
through which she was passing on a strip of dry land. 
 “I don’t like it,” she said to herself.  “I don’t like it, and she pinched her thin lips more tightly 
together.”

1 x 2 – 10 x 2 = – 9 x 2
